growth_story.headline: Oil savings paid for Timor-Leste's new state and a spending-led recovery, but as the oil ran out income per person fell back to its 2001 level.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Timor-Leste grew 8.3 percent a year in 1991–2000, an average that mixes steady growth with a 27.1 percent fall in 1999, the year of the independence vote, when withdrawing forces destroyed most government buildings, and a 77.1 percent rebound in 2000. In 2001–2008 growth averaged -0.6 percent a year: the new state lacked people, institutions and money, and unrest built up to an attempted coup in 2006. From 2007 the government spent well beyond what its oil savings could sustain, and growth picked up, averaging 3.2 percent a year in 2009–2016, though it tailed off after 2012 once spending levelled off. Since 2017 growth has averaged 0.2 percent a year, as a political impasse, COVID-19 and a cyclone hit the economy and the Bayu-Undan oil and gas field ran down and closed. Income per person peaked in 2021 and by 2025 was 39.8 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 2001.

threads.title: Destruction and a fragile start
threads.text: The country began with almost nothing: most public buildings, power and phone networks were destroyed around the 1999 vote. Between independence in 2002 and 2006 the new state struggled to get going, and growing discontent ended in an attempted coup in 2006.

since_last_year.text: Oil production ended in mid-2025, so the country now lives on its savings, not on new oil income. The economy outside oil still grew in 2025, helped by high public spending and more tourists, and Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in 2025 after joining the WTO in 2024. In the data, income per person rose 5.6 percent in 2025 after three years of decline.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Timor-Leste
citations.quote: Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) membership in 2025 and World Trade Organization (WTO) accession in 2024

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe an economy that grew in every year from 2022 to 2025, led by public spending. The data instead show income per person falling 21.6 percent in 2022, 19.0 percent in 2023 and 10.2 percent in 2024. The data's measure seems to include offshore oil output, which the sources leave out when they track the economy outside oil, so the fall follows the run-down of Bayu-Undan rather than what happened on shore. The same gap shows earlier: the data have income per person jumping 21.8 percent in 2019 and 29.2 percent in 2020, years the sources describe as political instability and COVID-19.
